title: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
summary: New U.S. restrictions could jeopardize billions in investment and force countries in the region to strike an increasingly difficult balance between Washington and Beijing.

The Trump administration’s proposal to[restrict](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/politics/trump-china-ai-chip-loophole.html) China’s access to advanced A.I. chips overseas rattled Southeast Asia on Tuesday, threatening a data center investment boom fueled by Chinese companies using the region to sidestep U.S. restrictions on Nvidia’s most powerful chips.


Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Singapore have become[offshore computing hubs](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/business/malaysia-data-center-china.html?searchResultPosition=1) for Chinese companies such as Alibaba and ByteDance. Data center operators in those countries provide the Chinese firms with remote access to advanced Nvidia chips they cannot buy directly or bring into China.


The strategy has drawn billions of dollars in investment to the region. But in Washington, officials seeking tighter controls on China’s A.I. sector have increasingly viewed data centers as a workaround that poses economic and national security risks.


Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was ousted last week after[revelations](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/technology/jensen-huang-nvidia-board.html) he had an affair with a woman who formed a Singaporean data center company called Megaspeed. U.S. authorities deemed the woman, Alice Huang, to be an asset for Chinese intelligence services, and they are investigating Megaspeed over allegations of smuggling chips to China. China has denied that Ms. Huang was spying for it.


Separately, Nvidia’s board of directors announced on Tuesday that it had established a committee to oversee “the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.” Nvidia’s board is engaged in a search for a permanent successor to Mr. Huang. The company’s interim chief executive,[Colette Kress](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/business/nvidia-colette-kress-jensen-huang.html) , is set to preside over the release of the company’s latest quarterly financial results later on Tuesday.


Shares of technology companies tumbled on Tuesday. In trading in Hong Kong, Alibaba fell more than 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell more than 7 percent and Z.AI declined more than 5 percent. In the United States, tech stocks slid lower, pulling the Nasdaq index down more than 1 percent. Nvidia shares faced choppy trading ahead of its earnings results, which are expected after the market closes.
